title: Verifier‑Assisted versus LLM‑Only Pre‑deployment Network‑Change Validation: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We evaluate whether adding a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier plus a bounded automated repair step improves the fraction of intent‑driven network‑change proposals that pass semantic validation compared with accepting a single LLM candidate. Under a preregistered paired design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) we executed 300 paired intents stratified by difficulty (100 per stratum) using a single shared LLM draw per pair (declared generator: gpt-5-mini) and a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Each pair compared baseline (accept the single shared candidate) against guarded (run validator and permit ≤1 constrained automated repair). Outcomes: baseline 299/300 unflagged passes (0.996667), guarded 300/300 (1.0); contingency counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; exact two‑sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (bootstrap seed = 1729, B = 10000). Execution consumed 301 model calls and invoked the permitted repair exactly once. Under the chosen shared_initial estimand, the single‑shot generator was near ceiling on this synthetic suite; deterministic repair produced one rescue. We archive preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts and interpret results with respect to estimand conditioning, validator semantics, repair budget, and operational deployment policies.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for network operations (NetOps) tasks including intent→configuration translation, template synthesis, and automated repair. For pre‑deployment network changes, semantic correctness properties—ordering/sequence constraints, reachability, and policy preservation—are operationally decisive and are not captured by surface syntactic checks alone. A common mitigation pattern is to pair a generative model with deterministic validation and a bounded repair operator (generate→validate→repair). The measurable value of such guarded pipelines depends critically on: (i) what is held constant when comparing pipelines (the estimand), (ii) the generator's single‑shot quality, (iii) the validator's semantic coverage, and (iv) the permitted repair budget and operator scope.

We preregistered a paired experiment (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) to isolate the deterministic rescue attributable to a verifier+bounded repair applied to the same single LLM candidate. For each intent the pipeline generated exactly one shared_initial candidate (one LLM draw reused across both conditions) and compared: baseline — accept that candidate without repair; guarded — run a deterministic validator and allow at most one constrained automated repair followed by re‑validation. This shared_initial conditioning corresponds to operational policies that restrict model calls for cost, latency, or governance reasons. Our primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in the unflagged verifier‑pass proportion (guarded − baseline) across N = 300 paired intents. The study was preregistered and executed with all artifacts archived to support reproducibility and forensic inspection.
sections.related_work:
Recent surveys and system papers document rapid progress on LLM use for NetOps tasks (intent translation, template synthesis, protocol test generation, and automated repair) and emphasize both opportunities and limitations of current approaches [1]–[3]. Tool‑augmented architectures (planner‑centric designs and ReAct‑style scaffolds) permit LLMs to call external validators or simulators to decompose complex multi‑step workflows; such designs improve practical handling of multi‑stage operations but conflate gains from tool use with gains from multiple model draws or interactive steering [4], [5]. Empirical studies report that integrating deterministic checks and generate→validate→repair scaffolds can materially improve surface correctness metrics relative to unconstrained generation, but reported magnitudes are dataset‑ and validator‑dependent [2], [6].

Two methodological themes motivate our design. First, prior evaluations often mix deterministic validation benefits with resampling or verifier‑guided regeneration; when model calls are unconstrained this mixing obscures how much rescue is attributable to the validator versus additional sampling from the generator [2], [4]. Second, many public NetOps benchmarks emphasize syntactic correctness over semantically rich invariants (reachability, sequencing, policy preservation), which limits operational generality of claims; the literature calls for verifier‑centric benchmarks that encode such invariants [3], [7]. Our study explicitly conditions on a single LLM draw per intent to measure bounded, post‑hoc deterministic rescue and to provide a practically relevant bound for policies that limit model calls.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The confirmatory protocol was preregistered before the main run; the primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in unflagged verifier‑pass proportion (guarded minus baseline) evaluated on N = 300 paired intents after applying prespecified inclusion/exclusion rules. The analysis executor and inference procedures (paired contingency counts, exact two‑sided McNemar, paired bootstrap percentile CI) were fixed prior to observing main‑run outcomes.

Task generation and stratification. Tasks were produced deterministically by a registered task generator into a synthetic topology suite stratified into low/medium/high difficulty (100 pairs per stratum). Each task encodes the natural‑language intent, initial and expected final device states, sequencing constraints (for example, 'must_be_down_for_fields'), preserve_unspecified_state invariants, and protected interfaces. Difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count) determined stratum membership and sampling.

Shared_initial generation and model configuration. To isolate deterministic validator/repair rescue from resampling effects we implemented the shared_initial estimand: for each pair the pipeline produced exactly one shared_initial candidate using the declared generator (gpt-5-mini) and reused that candidate verbatim for both conditions. Model configuration metadata recorded the requested model name (gpt-5-mini) and a conservative token/output budget; the adapter enforced a single shared generation per pair and a global repair budget of at most one constrained repair per pair.

Deterministic validator and repair operator. Semantic evaluation used a deterministic validator implementing a full_intent_constraint_validation rule set that checks sequencing invariants, required command counts, preservation of unspecified state, topology reachability invariants encoded by the synthetic suite, and forbidden‑template protections for protected interfaces. Scoring was binary: an unflagged candidate counted as a pass. The guarded pipeline permitted at most one automated repair attempt. The repair operator was a constrained localized edit routine (insertion or ordering fix) limited to addressing sequencing omissions or similar small, local defects; repairs were applied only when the validator deterministically flagged the candidate and were re‑validated deterministically.

Contamination controls and missingness rules. The preregistration included deterministic contamination detection (negative controls and invariant checks) and explicit inclusion/exclusion rules: exclude a pair only if both pipeline calls fail due to provider/infrastructure outage. Pairs with a single call failure would be retained under the primary executor handling; sensitivity analyses treat single‑call failures as failures. The confirmatory run produced no dual‑call outages and no exclusions.

Execution auditing and accounting. The run used an adapter implementing the preregistered shared_initial protocol and logged stage counts and provider call auditing. The execution accounting includes the number of completed episodes, model calls used, and the number of repair invocations. Deterministic reconciliation checks validated pair accounting consistency prior to analysis.

Analysis procedures. The primary confirmatory analysis computed the paired contingency counts (n11,n10,n01,n00), the absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline), an exact two‑sided McNemar test, and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI. The bootstrap parameters used in the archived analysis are seed = 1729 and B = 10000. Preplanned sensitivity analyses included failure‑as‑zero handling and stratum‑wise paired diagnostics labeled exploratory.
sections.results:
Execution integrity and accounting. The adapter completed the confirmatory run producing complete_pair_count = 300 under the shared_initial protocol. The run consumed 301 model calls (one repair stage invocation in addition to the 300 shared_initial generations) and recorded a single repair invocation across all guarded episodes. Deterministic reconciliation confirmed consistent episode accounting and absence of provider outages or excluded pairs.

Primary outcomes. Binary scoring produced baseline_success_count = 299 and guarded_success_count = 300 (baseline_rate = 0.9966667; guarded_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency counts are n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The exact two‑sided McNemar test operating on discordant counts (n10, n01) returned p = 1.0. The absolute paired improvement is 0.0033333 and the paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (seed = 1729, B = 10000) is [0.00, 0.01]. The minimal discordance (m = 1) constrains the sensitivity of the exact test and is the primary driver of the null inferential result.

Per‑stratum diagnostics. Stratified tallies show: low difficulty baseline = 100/100 and guarded = 100/100; medium baseline = 100/100 and guarded = 100/100; high baseline = 99/100 and guarded = 100/100. The single discordant instance is concentrated in the high stratum. These per‑stratum diagnostics confirm a near‑ceiling baseline in low and medium strata and attribute observed rescue to a single hard example in the high stratum.

Repair diagnostic and episode trace summary. The solitary discordant episode invoked the permitted constrained repair. Validator traces attribute the initial failure to a sequencing omission: the shared_initial candidate omitted an explicit 'admin down' before a VLAN/MTU change required by the intent. The constrained repair performed a single localized insertion restoring the required sequencing, after which the validator reported the corrected candidate as unflagged. Thus the guarded pipeline deterministically rescued one episode using the allowed bounded edit and one extra model/repair stage call.

Contamination and missingness. Preplanned contamination checks and negative controls did not flag anomalies. The missingness summary reports zero failed or unscorable episodes and zero excluded pairs under preregistered rules.

Operational cost. The guarded pipeline required one additional repair-stage call across 300 pairs (model_calls_used = 301; repair_invocations = 1), indicating low marginal model‑call cost for the deterministic rescue observed on this synthetic suite.

Statistical interpretation. Because exact McNemar inference depends only on discordant counts, the observed n10 = 1 and n01 = 0 yield p = 1.0 under a two‑sided exact test. The paired bootstrap CI bounds the absolute paired improvement to at most one percentage point under the recorded data and bootstrap parameters. These inferential statements apply strictly to the shared_initial estimand (one LLM draw per pair), the constrained repair budget (≤1 localized edit), the synthetic task distribution, and the declared model and validator.
sections.discussion:
Estimand alignment with operational policy. The shared_initial estimand operationalizes deployment policies that bound model calls per change and thus isolates deterministic rescue that can be achieved by post‑hoc validation and bounded correction of the same candidate. This contrasts with evaluations that permit resampling, verifier‑guided regeneration, or interactive steering; those alternative estimands typically show larger gains but reflect different operational cost and governance tradeoffs.

Ceiling effects and the absent calibration pilot. The preregistered design targeted detection of a 10 percentage‑point absolute improvement with power ≈0.8 based on an intended pilot to estimate discordance. The optional pilot was not executed; consequently the main run encountered a near‑ceiling baseline (299/300) and observed minimal discordance (m = 1), reducing power to detect small absolute differences. This practical outcome illustrates the utility of small calibration pilots when generator performance is uncertain relative to task difficulty.

Validator coverage and failure‑mode dependence. The single observed failure mode (sequencing omission) is only one of several classes relevant in real networks (reachability violations, ACL semantics, forbidden ACL removal, resource/configuration interactions). The practical benefit of a guarded pipeline increases with the prevalence of failure modes the validator can express. Thus observed marginal utility depends on the joint distribution of failure modes in deployment and on validator expressiveness.

Repair budget and operator design. Our bounded repair operator was intentionally conservative (one localized insertion/edit) to measure deterministic rescue under modest automation privileges. Larger or iterative repair strategies, richer edit operators, or verifier‑guided regeneration would constitute different interventions with potentially larger rescue effects but higher model‑call cost and distinct operational risk profiles. The archived repair trace for the rescued episode provides a concrete example that operators can inspect when deciding permitted edit scopes in production.

Implications for CI/CD and deployment. Organizations that tightly constrain model calls can use the shared_initial protocol to bound the deterministic rescue obtainable from a verifier+bounded repair step applied to a single candidate. Conversely, organizations prepared to permit resampling or interactive repair should evaluate a different estimand that measures the combined benefit of validation plus additional generator variance exploitation. Our execution accounting (one repair invocation across 300 pairs) quantifies the low marginal runtime cost of bounded deterministic rescue in the present synthetic setting but does not generalize to richer repair regimes or different task distributions.

Limitations and recommended follow‑ups. This study used a synthetic task suite, one generator configuration (gpt-5-mini), and a single deterministic validator design; external validity to production networks, alternative LLMs, and richer validators is limited. A small calibration pilot prior to the main run would have produced tighter sample‑size calibration given the observed near‑ceiling baseline. Follow‑up experiments should preregister alternative estimands that permit resampling or iterative verifier‑guided repair and should evaluate validator coverage sensitivity by injecting targeted failure‑mode classes (reachability, ACL semantics) at scale.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired comparison that conditioned on a single LLM draw per intent to measure deterministic rescue offered by a deterministic validator plus at most one constrained automated repair. On 300 synthetic intent pairs using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 the baseline single‑shot generator passed semantic validation in 299/300 cases and the guarded pipeline passed in 300/300, yielding an absolute paired improvement of 0.00333 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.01]). Deterministic repair produced one rescue; marginal model‑call cost was minimal in this run (one extra repair call). Under operational policies that limit model calls, the shared_initial estimand provides a conservative, policy‑aligned bound on what deterministic validation and bounded repair can rescue. We release the preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and to enable targeted follow‑ups that vary estimand conditioning, validator coverage, model strength, and repair budgets.

limitations: Synthetic benchmark: tasks and topologies were generated deterministically; real‑world heterogeneity may expose different failure modes and increase the marginal utility of validation and repair.
Single model and validator: the study evaluated only gpt-5-mini and a single deterministic validator design; results may not generalize to other LLMs or richer/diverse validators.

Ceiling effect: baseline single‑shot performance was near 100% on this suite (299/300), producing limited discordance and reduced power to detect small absolute improvements relative to larger pre‑specified targets.
Pilot not executed: the preregistered optional pilot for discordance estimation and power calibration was not run; no post‑preregistration recalculation of required sample size was performed.

Estimand conditioning: the shared_initial protocol conditions on a single LLM candidate per intent and therefore does not measure verifier benefit that would arise from allowing independent alternative LLM candidates per condition (resampling or iterative generation).
Repair budget: the guarded condition permitted at most one constrained automated repair per pair; larger or iterative repair strategies may yield different outcomes.
